sentences.zh: 上賢貫高為人能立然諾，使泄公具告之，曰：「張王已出。」

translations.literal: The Emperor admired Guan Gao as a man who could keep his word, and sent Xie Gong to inform him fully, saying: 'King Zhang has been released.'
translations.idiomatic: The Emperor admired Guan Gao as a man who kept his word. He sent Xie Gong to tell him, 'King Zhang has been released.'

sentences.zh: 因赦貫高。

translations.literal: He then pardoned Guan Gao.
translations.idiomatic: He also pardoned Guan Gao.

sentences.zh: 貫高喜曰：「吾王審出乎？」

translations.literal: Guan Gao said joyfully: 'Has my king truly been released?'
translations.idiomatic: Guan Gao was overjoyed. 'Has my king truly been released?' he asked.

sentences.zh: 泄公曰：「然。」

translations.literal: Xie Gong said: 'Yes.'
translations.idiomatic: Xie Gong said, 'He has.'

sentences.zh: 泄公曰：「上多足下，故赦足下。」

translations.literal: Xie Gong said: 'The Emperor admires you, and therefore pardons you.'
translations.idiomatic: Xie Gong added, 'The Emperor admires your character, and so he pardons you as well.'

sentences.zh: 貫高曰：「所以不死一身無餘者，白張王不反也。

translations.literal: Guan Gao said: 'The reason I clung to life with nothing left was to clear King Zhang of the charge of rebellion.
translations.idiomatic: Guan Gao said, 'The only reason I held on to life when I had nothing left was to prove that King Zhang did not rebel.

sentences.zh: 今王已出，吾責已塞，死不恨矣。

translations.literal: Now the king has been released, and my duty is fulfilled. I can die without regret.
translations.idiomatic: Now the king has been freed, and my duty is fulfilled. I can die without regret.

sentences.zh: 且人臣有篡殺之名，何面目復事上哉！

translations.literal: Moreover, as a minister who bears the name of plotting assassination, with what face could I serve the Emperor again!
translations.idiomatic: Besides, as a minister who bears the disgrace of plotting assassination, how could I ever face the Emperor again?

sentences.zh: 縱上不殺我，我不愧於心乎？」

translations.literal: Even if the Emperor does not kill me, would I not be ashamed in my own heart?'
translations.idiomatic: Even if the Emperor spares my life, would I not be ashamed before my own conscience?'

sentences.zh: 乃仰絕骯，遂死。

translations.literal: He then threw back his head and severed his own throat, and died.
translations.idiomatic: He threw back his head and cut his own throat, and so he died.

sentences.zh: 當此之時，名聞天下。

translations.literal: At that time, his fame was known throughout the realm.
translations.idiomatic: His name became renowned throughout the realm.

sentences.zh: 張敖已出，以尚魯元公主故，封為宣平侯。

translations.literal: After Zhang Ao was released, because he was married to Princess Luyuan, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xuanping.
translations.idiomatic: After his release, Zhang Ao was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xuanping on account of his marriage to Princess Luyuan.

sentences.zh: 於是上賢張王諸客，以鉗奴從張王入關，無不為諸侯相、郡守者。

translations.literal: Thereupon the Emperor admired the retainers of King Zhang, who as collared slaves had followed the king through the Pass—not one of them failed to become a chancellor of a feudal lord or a commandery governor.
translations.idiomatic: The Emperor admired the retainers of King Zhang who had disguised themselves as collared slaves to follow the king to the capital. Every one of them was eventually appointed chancellor of a feudal state or governor of a commandery.

sentences.zh: 及孝惠、高后、文帝、孝景時，張王客子孫皆得為二千石。

translations.literal: Through the reigns of Emperor Xiaohui, Empress Dowager Gao, Emperor Wen, and Emperor Xiaojing, the descendants of King Zhang's retainers all attained the rank of two-thousand-bushel officials.
translations.idiomatic: Through the reigns of Emperor Hui, Empress Dowager Gao, Emperor Wen, and Emperor Jing, the descendants of King Zhang's retainers all attained the rank of two-thousand-bushel officials.

sentences.zh: 張敖，高后六年薨。

translations.literal: Zhang Ao died in the sixth year of Empress Dowager Gao's reign.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Ao died in the sixth year of Empress Dowager Gao's regency.

sentences.zh: 子偃為魯元王。

translations.literal: His son Yan became King of Luyuan.
translations.idiomatic: His son Zhang Yan became the King of Luyuan.

sentences.zh: 以母呂后女故，呂后封為魯元王。

translations.literal: Because his mother was a daughter of Empress Lu, Empress Lu enfeoffed him as King of Luyuan.
translations.idiomatic: Because his mother was a daughter of Empress Lu, the Empress enfeoffed him as King of Luyuan.

sentences.zh: 元王弱，兄弟少，乃封張敖他姬子二人：壽為樂昌侯，侈為信都侯。

translations.literal: The King of Luyuan was young and had few brothers, so two sons of Zhang Ao by other concubines were enfeoffed: Shou as Marquis of Lechang, and Chi as Marquis of Xindu.
translations.idiomatic: Since the young king had few brothers, two sons of Zhang Ao by other consorts were also enfeoffed: Shou as Marquis of Lechang and Chi as Marquis of Xindu.

sentences.zh: 高后崩，諸呂無道，大臣誅之，而廢魯元王及樂昌侯、信諸侯。

translations.literal: When Empress Dowager Gao died, the Lu clan acted without righteousness. The great ministers punished them and abolished the King of Luyuan, the Marquis of Lechang, and the Marquis of Xindu.
translations.idiomatic: After Empress Dowager Gao died, the Lu clan overreached and was destroyed by the senior ministers, who also deposed the King of Luyuan and stripped the Marquises of Lechang and Xindu of their titles.

sentences.zh: 孝文帝即位，復封故魯元王偃為南宮侯，續張氏。

translations.literal: When Emperor Xiaowen ascended the throne, he re-enfeoffed the former King of Luyuan, Yan, as Marquis of Nangong, continuing the Zhang line.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen ascended the throne, he re-enfeoffed the former King of Luyuan, Zhang Yan, as Marquis of Nangong to continue the Zhang family line.

sentences.zh: 太史公曰：張耳、陳餘，世傳所稱賢者；

translations.literal: The Grand Historian says: Zhang Er and Chen Yu were called worthy men by tradition throughout the ages;
translations.idiomatic: The Grand Historian remarks: Zhang Er and Chen Yu were called worthy men in the traditions handed down through the ages.

sentences.zh: 其賓客廝役，莫非天下俊桀，所居國無不取卿相者。

translations.literal: Their retainers and servants were all outstanding talents of the realm; wherever they settled, they invariably rose to the rank of minister or chancellor.
translations.idiomatic: Their retainers and attendants were without exception the most brilliant men of their day, and wherever they settled they invariably rose to the highest offices.

sentences.zh: 然張耳、陳餘始居約時，相然信以死，豈顧問哉。

translations.literal: Yet when Zhang Er and Chen Yu first lived in humble straits, they pledged their faith to each other unto death—who could have questioned their sincerity?
translations.idiomatic: Yet when Zhang Er and Chen Yu first lived in poverty together, they pledged their faith to each other unto death. Who could have doubted their sincerity then?

sentences.zh: 及據國爭權，卒相滅亡，何鄉者相慕用之誠，後相倍之戾也！

translations.literal: But once they held states and fought for power, they ended by destroying each other. How sincere was their earlier admiration, and how bitter their later betrayal!
translations.idiomatic: But once they held states and contended for power, they ended by destroying each other. How fervent was their early devotion, and how savage their later betrayal!

sentences.zh: 豈非以勢利交哉？

translations.literal: Was this not friendship based on power and profit?
translations.idiomatic: Was their bond not, in the end, a friendship founded upon power and self-interest?

sentences.zh: 名譽雖高，賓客雖盛，所由殆與大伯、延陵季子異矣。

translations.literal: Though their fame was great and their followers many, the path they followed was surely different from that of Taibo and Jizi of Yanling.
translations.idiomatic: Though their fame was great and their following numerous, the path they walked was far removed from that of Taibo and Jizi of Yanling.
